newsitem.title: CANADA: Thiessen says Canada's CPI rise may be overstated.
newsitem.headline: Thiessen says Canada's CPI rise may be overstated.

text.p: Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen said on Tuesday that Canada's consumer price index might be overstated by half of one percentage point each year, substantially less than in the United States.

In testimony before the Senate Banking Committee, he was asked if Canada's monitoring of inflation might be influenced by a congressionally appointed U.S. panel that found the U.S. CPI overstated inflation by 1.1 points a year.
The calculation of CPI is important because it is used for programs such as old-age pensions in both countries, for taxation in the United States and for many wage settlements in the private sector.
Trimming increases in the CPI would therefore result in big spending reductions and has become a major political issue in the United States.

Thiessen said the U.S. study generated a lot of interest in Canada, but that the government agency Statistics Canada, which compiles the Canadian index, found that the Canadian CPI was less skewed than the U.S. one.
"A lot of the biases that were discovered are biases that either don't exist here or Statistics Canada has reduced them to a very low level," he said.
But he pointed to a similar study at the Bank of Canada in 1993 that found an overestimation, even if less than in the United States.
"We found a bias in the consumer price index that was at the maximum of one half of one percent(age point)," he said.

"We're going to be looking at that again, because there's some interesting stuff that's come out of this American study, and it may well be that the bias is slightly larger than that, but probably not much.

"Basically it looks to us that the consumer price index in Canada is better constructed than the one in the United States and therefore the kind of estimate of one percentage point a year doesn't look to us to be the case here in Canada."

Bank of Canada Deputy Governor Charles Freedman explained afterward that if for example the increase in Canada's CPI were 1-3/4 percent, the actual increase would be around 1-1/4 percent if it was overstated by the amount found in the Bank of Canada study.

The most recent inflation figures showed a 2.2 percent annual rise in the overall Canadian CPI and a 1.8 percent rise, if food and energy were excluded. The bank excludes those items as well as the effect of indirect taxes in targeting inflation of one to three percent a year.
In the United States, the annual overall rise is 3.0 percent and 2.5 percent excluding food and energy.

Asked by reporters if readjusting the way the CPI were calculated would eliminate the difference in the two countries' inflation rates and affect the exchange rate outlook, Thiessen said: "I don't think it eliminates all the differential, but hypothetically, if you could somehow eliminate all the differential, that would make a difference."

"It's nonetheless the case that given they are operating at full potential and we're not there yet, you've got this situation where the inflation risk in the U.S. has got to be on the upside and ours has got to be on the downside.
"That has got to have an influence on the outlook for the currency over time."
